introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2023. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Illustrate and explain the pattern of latitudinal distribution of precipitation on the earth's surface.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Precipitation** (rain, drizzle, snow, hail) varies with latitude in a repeated pattern of wet and dry belts, which is shown in the diagram below. It is controlled mainly by the **global pressure and wind belts**, which determine where air rises (cooling, condensation, rain) and where air sinks (warming, drying, little rain).

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

**The pattern and its explanation.**

1. **Equatorial belt (about 0 to 10 degrees N and S): the highest precipitation.** Strong solar heating of the land and sea produces very hot, moist air, which rises in the **equatorial low-pressure zone (the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, ITCZ)**, where the trade winds meet. The rising air cools, the water vapour condenses and heavy **convectional rainfall** falls, often almost daily in the afternoon (the Congo Basin and southern Cameroon, the Amazon Basin and Indonesia). Warm air holds much more water vapour, so the supply of moisture is very large.
2. **Sub-tropical belts (about 20 to 35 degrees N and S): low precipitation.** The air that rose at the equator spreads out at height, cools, and sinks in the **sub-tropical high-pressure belts** (the descending limb of the Hadley cell). Sinking air is compressed and warmed, so its relative humidity falls and clouds do not form. The hot deserts (the Sahara, the Kalahari, the Arabian and Australian deserts) lie here. The north of Cameroon already shows the transition towards this drier belt.
3. **Mid-latitudes (about 40 to 60 degrees N and S): a second, smaller maximum.** At the **polar front**, mild moist tropical air carried by the westerlies meets cold polar air. The warm air is forced to rise over the cold air and depressions form, so that frontal (cyclonic) rainfall is frequent throughout the year (north-west Europe, the west coasts of Canada and Chile). The amounts are lower than at the equator because the air is cooler and holds less vapour.
4. **Polar areas: very low precipitation.** The air is very cold and holds very little water vapour, and the **polar high pressure** produces sinking air, so that polar regions are cold deserts with small amounts of precipitation, mostly as snow.

**Modifications of the simple pattern.** The belts move north and south with the overhead sun (the ITCZ migrates seasonally), so that the tropical savanna has a wet and a dry season and monsoon areas have strong seasonal rains. The pattern is also disturbed by distance from the sea (continentality), ocean currents (warm or cold), relief (rain on windward slopes, rain shadow on leeward slopes) and the distribution of land and sea, so that the real pattern is less regular than the model.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Examine any TWO ways in which man is responsible for urban heat island.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
An **urban heat island** is the zone of higher air temperature found in a town or city compared with the surrounding rural areas; the difference can reach several degrees Celsius and is greatest on calm, clear nights. Two ways in which human activities are responsible are the following.

**1. Replacement of natural surfaces by buildings and paved surfaces.** People remove vegetation and soil and replace them with concrete, asphalt, bricks and metal roofs. These materials have a **low albedo** (they reflect little of the sunshine) and a **high thermal capacity and conductivity**, so they absorb a lot of heat during the day, store it and release it slowly at night, which keeps the city warm after sunset. Vegetation and open water, which cool the air by **evapotranspiration**, are lost, and rainwater is quickly removed by drains and gutters, so that less energy is used up in evaporation and more is used to heat the air. Tall buildings close together (the "urban canyon" effect) also trap the heat reflected between the walls and reduce the amount of heat that escapes to the sky and the cooling effect of the wind.

**2. Release of waste heat and pollutants by human activities.** Heat is released directly into the air by **vehicle engines, factories, power stations, air conditioners and domestic cooking and heating** (anthropogenic heat), and it is concentrated in a small area. Cities also emit **dust, smoke and gases (including carbon dioxide)**, which form a pollution dome over the town. This dome absorbs and re-radiates part of the long-wave heat leaving the city, in a local greenhouse effect, and the smog traps the warm air close to the ground.

Other ways (not required) include the reduction of air movement by buildings, so that the warm air is not replaced by cooler air, and the removal of green spaces for housing and roads, as in the fast growth of cities such as Douala and Yaounde. **Conclusion:** the urban heat island is mainly the result of the way people change the surface and the energy balance of the town.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) How can form and intensity of precipitation influence the rate of interception?

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Interception** is the part of precipitation that is caught and held by the leaves, branches and stems of plants (the canopy), and by litter, and which returns to the atmosphere by evaporation without reaching the ground. The **rate of interception** (the proportion of the precipitation that is intercepted) depends on the type of vegetation and also on the form and the intensity of the precipitation.

**Influence of the form of precipitation.**

- **Rain.** Raindrops fall onto the leaf surfaces, wet them and fill the small water stores on the canopy; the water is later evaporated. Fine **drizzle** has small drops that are held easily on leaves and so a large share of it is intercepted.
- **Snow.** Snow can be held on the branches, especially of conifers, and can be lost by sublimation and melting without reaching the ground, so interception can be high at first. Heavy wet snow can also break the branches and fall off in lumps.
- **Hail.** Hailstones are heavy and bounce off or knock off leaves, so a small share is intercepted, although the stones may remain and melt on the ground.
- **Fog and mist drip (occult precipitation).** In cloud forests and on mountain slopes (such as the highlands of Cameroon), the fine droplets of the fog condense on leaves and drip to the ground, so the vegetation may add water instead of only intercepting it.

**Influence of the intensity of precipitation.**

- Each canopy has a limited **storage capacity**, which is the amount of water that the leaf surfaces can hold. In a **light shower** (low intensity), the rain is spread over a long time, the canopy does not become saturated and the water evaporates, so a **high proportion** (a large percentage) of the rain is intercepted and may never reach the soil.
- In a **heavy or intense storm** (high intensity), the storage capacity is filled quickly. The excess water drips from the leaves (**throughfall**) and runs down the branches and trunk (**stemflow**), so that most of the rain reaches the ground. The percentage intercepted is therefore **small**. Large raindrops also hit the leaves, shake the canopy and make the water fall faster.
- The **duration** of the rain matters too: in a long rainfall the canopy remains saturated, and the interception loss is only what is evaporated during the rainfall.

**Conclusion:** interception is greatest (in percentage) when the precipitation is light, short and in a form that is easily held on the plants (fine rain, drizzle or snow on conifers), and it is least during intense, long-lasting rainstorms and hail.
